title: The development of humour in children

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: If you try telling a language-based joke to a toddler, they’re likely to stare at you blankly. Babies can be an even tougher audience, frequently ignoring your impressions of animals but breaking into giggles unexpectedly at other times. My two-year-old son has recently started grabbing my nose and pretending to throw it in the kitchen bin while laughing hysterically. It may not be a joke that I’m likely to try at my next dinner party, but it shows that his sense of humour is developing. Children find different situations funny at different ages, although human beings are all so unique that ticking off specific, age-related stages as a child grows up is clearly not feasible.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The main element necessary for the development of a sense of humour is socialisation. Human beings typically react to and laugh at actions and situations together – a process that effectively starts as soon as a baby can engage in eye contact and smiling. The psychologist Lev Vygotsky believed that humorous social interactions of this type actually facilitate a child’s cognitive development. However, a child needs to possess a few basic cognitive skills in order to make jokes in the first place (beyond just pulling a funny face).

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Almost all types of humour require a realisation of incongruity or mismatch between a concept and a situation. In other words, we laugh when things surprise us because they seem not to belong together. Take the following joke, for example: ‘A horse walks into a bar and the barman says ‘Why the long face!’’. This is partly funny because horses don’t normally walk into bars. But the punchline ‘Why the long face?’ is amusing because at first we understand it to mean that the horse is sad, but we don’t know why. We then suddenly realise that the expression has another meaning – horses also literally have long faces. It may therefore seem that language is a prerequisite for humour. Infants without language and younger children with limited language typically enjoy physical humour, such as a game of peek-a-boo, where someone pretends to hide and then jumps out. But even jokes like these, involving fewer cognitive skills than language-based jokes, are about a realisation of incompatibility or incongruity. Peek-a-boo has an element of surprise – someone suddenly appearing out of nowhere. Indeed, many researchers argue that it is communication that is key and that humour actually facilitates the process of learning a language.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Imagination is crucial for spotting incongruity. It helps children place themselves somewhere different, to enact social roles that they normally wouldn’t, and even to pretend that someone’s nose has come off, as my son delights in doing. Imagination begins to appear in children at around 12-18 months of age. Interestingly, this corresponds with the time when children are starting to copy parents’ jokes - making them more active in the production of their own brand of humour. Indeed, children as young as seven months can deliberately repeat any behaviours that elicit laughs, such as a funny face or a game of peek-a-boo. Imagination is also important for a child to eventually be able to produce jokes of their own. This generally starts with either object-based jokes, such as placing underwear on the head, or conceptual ones, such as claiming ‘the cat says moo’. When thinking up jokes, children often draw inspiration from whatever they are learning about, such as how to sit and eat with others, or how to share. Importantly, joking about something is a way of processing the social rules associated with it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Another cognitive skill that helps children develop humour is an awareness of how the mind works, for example in relation to deception and sarcasm. Realising that various people in a group may have different knowledge or mental states - and that some can have false beliefs or be deceived – is important. For example, when parents pretend to be oblivious to a child sneaking up to scare them, this is actually an example of a child comprehending deception. Indeed, some research has shown that this knowledge is crucial for children to make sense of jokes involving sarcasm. One study showed that some children as young as three (but typically around five) are able to comprehend such forms of humour. In the experiment, children aged between three and six watched a puppet show and were asked questions about what they saw. During the show, one puppet broke a plate and another commented, ‘your mum will be very happy’. Some of the children laughed, realising that this wasn’t literal and that the mother would in fact not be happy at all.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other research argues that the understanding of sarcasm and other humorous devices develops through experience with humour itself rather than perspective-taking or knowledge of deception. Joking is social and cultural, so a part of this process is having to learn through social interaction. Once children have developed a basic understanding of others and an imagination, they can use their humour to explore possible and actual feelings. For example, by hurling invisible food around and gleefully yelling ‘I’m messy’, a child can get a parent to act out a scenario in which they pretend to be annoyed. The joke enables the child to explore anger safely.
